title: The Mountain of Light Changes Hands
subtitle: The Koh-i-Noor diamond from the Lahore treasury to a London workshop, 1849–1852
intro: On 29 March 1849, at the end of the Second Anglo-Sikh War, the ten-year-old Maharaja Duleep Singh signed the terms that ended his kingdom. The Treaty of Lahore annexed the Punjab to British India. Its third article dealt with a single object: the gem called the Koh-i-Noor, which Maharaja Ranjit Singh had taken from Shah Shuja, was to be surrendered by the Maharaja of Lahore to the Queen of England. Lord Dalhousie, the Governor-General, insisted that the stone go to the Crown and not to the East India Company. The directors in London objected, and his letters home show him defending the choice for months.

The stone already had a long history of seizure, and much of it is disputed. The diamond Babur describes in his memoirs has been identified with the Koh-i-Noor by some writers and denied by others; Valentine Ball and Nevil Story-Maskelyne argued the point in Nature in 1891. Nadir Shah carried it from Delhi to Persia after sacking the city in 1739. It passed to the Durrani rulers of Afghanistan and then to Shah Shuja. On 1 June 1813, by the account in the Lahore court chronicle of Sohan Lal Suri, Shah Shuja surrendered it to Ranjit Singh at Lahore. Ranjit wore it in an armlet at court. The sources for that phase include Persian chronicles, the recollections of the Kashmiri munshi Mohan Lal and stories told of Ranjit's minister Fakir Azizuddin. They are context here, not entries.

This chapter follows the stone over three years. It went from the Lahore treasury, where the Scottish surgeon John Login kept the Toshakhana, to Dalhousie's own body: he carried it to Bombay sewn into a belt. From Bombay HMS Medea took it to England in 1850, with cholera aboard, a hostile reception at Mauritius and a storm on the way. It was presented to Queen Victoria on 3 July 1850, in the East India Company's 250th anniversary year. At the Great Exhibition of 1851 crowds found it a disappointment. In July 1852 it was recut in a London workshop, the Duke of Wellington making the first cut. The honest record is mostly letters, official minutes and receipts, newspapers, scientific papers and one later memoir; only Queen Victoria and Henry Cole kept diaries that touch it. The form tags say so.

The people whose stone it was are the hardest to hear. No firsthand Sikh court account of the handover in 1849 was found for this chapter. Duleep Singh's own words survive only from later years: through Lady Login's memoir of 1890, which recalls him handing the recut stone back to the Queen in 1854, and through his letters of the 1880s, which call the annexation an injustice. Two well-known stories are later traditions. One is that John Lawrence left the diamond in a waistcoat pocket and his bearer found it in a tin box. The other is the 'curse' said to fall on any man who wears it. The anecdote is labelled as such in its entry. The curse is a legend, recorded by the Royal Collection as the reason only queens have worn the stone.

A coda records positions, not verdicts. Duleep Singh protested in 1882. Pakistan's prime minister asked for the stone in 1976, and Afghanistan's Taliban government claimed it in 2000. Iranian commentators have pointed to Nadir Shah's ownership. In India, Sikh bodies have claimed it and Parliament has raised it more than once. In April 2016 India's Solicitor General told the Supreme Court that the stone had been given rather than stolen; the government then said it would still seek its return by amicable means. The British government has repeatedly declined to return it. The diamond, recut to 105.6 metric carats, is now in the crown made for Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother in 1937 and is kept in the Tower of London.
calendar_note: All dates in the chapter are Gregorian and need no conversion. Two other kinds of measurement can mislead. Carats: nineteenth-century sources give the uncut stone as about 186 (186 1/16) old English carats, equal to about 190.3 modern metric carats. The recut stone is variously given as 108.93 old carats or 105.6 metric carats. These describe one result in two units; they are not rival measurements. Dates by mail: Dalhousie's letters from India took five to seven weeks to reach Britain, so reactions in London lag events in Lahore by a month or more. The 1813 handover to Ranjit Singh, mentioned only in the introduction, is recorded in sources that used Vikrami and Hijri dating. The Gregorian date given there is the one historians usually cite.

eyes.name: James Andrew Broun-Ramsay, 1st Marquess of Dalhousie
eyes.role: Governor-General of India (1848–1856), aged 36–38; architect of the annexation of the Punjab
eyes.side: British India / East India Company government
eyes.where: Ferozepur and Lahore, then on the road to Bombay; later Calcutta and Delhi

waypoints.label: Bombay, 1 February 1850: deposits it in the treasury

eyes.vantage_label: the man who took it for the Crown
eyes.authenticity: Private letters to his friend Sir George Couper, edited by J. G. A. Baird as Private Letters of the Marquess of Dalhousie (1910); official minutes in the National Archives of India; letters to Queen Victoria in the Royal Archives. The private letters are candid but were selected by the editor.
eyes.bio: A Scottish peer who became Governor-General at 35 and annexed the Punjab on his own authority. He treated the Koh-i-Noor as a trophy owed to the Queen herself, not to the Company, and carried it to Bombay on his own person. His private letters show pride, impatience with the directors in London and little sympathy for the boy who lost it.

sources.title: Private Letters of the Marquess of Dalhousie (ed. J. G. A. Baird, 1910), catalogue record
The Conversation: 'No ordinary diamond' (quotes Dalhousie to Couper, 1849)
National Archives of India: Dalhousie minute ordering information on the history of the Koh-i-noor, 22 December 1849

eyes.name: Maharaja Duleep Singh
eyes.role: Last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire, aged 10 at the surrender; later an exile in Britain
eyes.side: Sikh Empire (Lahore Darbar); later a British pensioner and, in the 1880s, a protester against Britain
eyes.vantage_label: the owner who signed it away as a child
eyes.authenticity: No writing by the boy from 1849 survives in this chapter's sources. His signature is on the Treaty. His 1854 words come through Lady Login's later memoir. His own letters of the 1880s, including one to The Times in 1882, were printed at the time.
eyes.bio: The youngest son of Ranjit Singh, placed on the throne at five, deposed at ten, and sent to England at fifteen after converting to Christianity. For decades he lived as a favourite of Queen Victoria. In the 1880s he turned against Britain, demanding his estates and kingdom back. He was stopped at Aden on his way to India and returned to the Sikh faith there. His changing attitude to the stone is the moral centre of the story.

sources.title: Historic Royal Palaces: Duleep Singh
Historic Royal Palaces source booklet (Duleep Singh letter to The Times, 1882)

eyes.name: Sir John Spencer Login
eyes.role: Scottish surgeon of the Bengal Army; from April 1849 governor of the Lahore citadel and keeper of the Toshakhana (state treasury); later guardian of Duleep Singh
eyes.authenticity: His letters to his wife from Lahore in 1849 were printed in Lady Login's Sir John Login and Duleep Singh (1890). That book prints only extracts, chosen by his widow.
eyes.bio: Login inventoried Ranjit Singh's treasury, the jewels, shawls and arms of a fallen court, and held the Koh-i-Noor until Dalhousie came for it. He then became the boy Maharaja's guardian. His letters are a rare inside view of the treasury at the moment it changed hands.

sources.title: John Spencer Login (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Lena Campbell, Lady Login
eyes.role: Wife of John Login; companion to Duleep Singh in England, 1854
eyes.vantage_label: in the room in 1854, writing decades later
eyes.authenticity: Sir John Login and Duleep Singh (London, 1890), compiled from memory and family papers more than thirty years after the events. The words she gives to Duleep Singh and to the Queen are her recollection, not a transcript.
eyes.bio: Lena Login watched Duleep Singh grow up and was present when Queen Victoria put the recut diamond into his hands. She wrote after his break with the Crown, defending her husband's guardianship, and her account of the 1854 scene became the standard version.

sources.title: The Tribune: How Duleep Singh handed it to the Queen (summarises Lady Login)

eyes.name: John Laird Mair Lawrence (later 1st Baron Lawrence)
eyes.role: Member of the Board of Administration of the Punjab, 1849; later Viceroy of India
eyes.vantage_label: a custodian in a later anecdote
eyes.authenticity: Lawrence left no diary entry about the stone. The waistcoat-pocket story is a later anecdote passed down in Anglo-Indian tradition and retold in biographies. A 2022 survey, drawing on Dalrymple and Anand, notes no contemporary evidence for it. It also does not fit the documented December 1849 handover to Dalhousie.
eyes.bio: A blunt, hard-working Punjab administrator, younger brother of Sir Henry Lawrence. The Board of Administration he sat on oversaw the annexed province. The famous story of his absent-mindedness has outlived any record behind it.

sources.title: R. Bosworth Smith, Life of Lord Lawrence, vol. 1 (1883), PDF
The Week (2022): How a forgetful British civil servant nearly lost Koh-i-Noor

eyes.name: Captain James Ramsay
eyes.role: Army officer and Dalhousie's kinsman, one of two officers who escorted the stone to England
eyes.where: Aboard HMS Medea, Bombay to Plymouth

waypoints.label: East India House, Leadenhall Street, 2 July 1850

eyes.authenticity: His letters to Dalhousie are in the National Archives of India (Foreign Department series 72–92 of 1850, 'History and Conveyance to England of the Koh-i-noor'). One is catalogued as written from Bombay Harbour. The catalogue's date for it, 14 June 1850, does not fit a ship that sailed in April and may be a docketing date. Colonel Frederick Mackeson's letters, which differ from Ramsay's on some details, are in the same series.
eyes.bio: Ramsay and Lieutenant-Colonel Frederick Mackeson held the keys to the box. Their orders were known only to them and Commander William Lockyer, the Medea's captain. Through them the voyage is documented by letters, and Lockyer's log was not consulted for this chapter.

sources.title: National Archives of India: Ramsay to Dalhousie, Medea arrived, gem safely embarked (No. 89)
National Archives of India: receipt on delivery of the Koh-i-noor by Mackeson and Ramsay
Indian Culture portal: Koh-i-noor (NAI documents)

eyes.name: Queen Victoria
eyes.role: Queen of the United Kingdom, aged 31–35
eyes.where: Buckingham Palace and the Crystal Palace, London
eyes.authenticity: Her journal survives in the Royal Archives, much of it in Princess Beatrice's later edited transcript. The entries used here were not printed before 1929, so they are given as digests only, from the Royal Collection and from Dalrymple and Anand's quotations.
eyes.bio: Victoria received the stone as a gift of conquest. She found it disappointing at first, approved the costly recutting, and wore it as a brooch. Her journal shows her fond of Duleep Singh and uneasy about the stone in his presence, and she later wrote that she disliked wearing it.

sources.title: Royal Collection Trust: The Koh-i-nûr armlet c. 1830
Royal Collection Trust: Winterhalter, The Maharaja Duleep Singh, 1854
Victorian Web: review of Dalrymple and Anand, Koh-i-Noor

eyes.name: Sir Henry Cole
eyes.role: Civil servant and one of the chief organisers of the Great Exhibition; later first director of the South Kensington Museum
eyes.where: The Crystal Palace, Hyde Park; later South Kensington
eyes.authenticity: Cole kept a daily diary for most of his adult life; the manuscripts are in the National Art Library at the V&A. The entries here are those transcribed by the V&A.
eyes.bio: Cole ran much of the Exhibition's practical business. His terse diary records the day the stone came out of its cage. His entry is the only one in this chapter by someone who held the uncut stone in his hand and wrote about it that day.

sources.title: V&A blog: Henry Cole and the Koh-i-Noor Diamond

eyes.name: The Times (London), unsigned reporters
eyes.authenticity: Contemporary dated reports. The 1851 items are quoted by the V&A. The 19 July 1852 account of the first cut is known here from a full reprint in a New Zealand paper.
eyes.bio: The Times reported the stone's disappointing showing, the efforts to light it better and the start of the recutting. Its words set the tone that pushed Prince Albert to have the stone recut.

sources.title: V&A blog (quotes The Times, 13 and 16 June, 13 October 1851)
New Zealand Spectator, 8 December 1852, reprinting The Times of 19 July 1852 (Papers Past)

eyes.name: The Illustrated London News, unsigned writers and engravers
eyes.authenticity: Contemporary dated issues; the engraving of 31 May 1851 is reproduced by the V&A from the National Art Library copy.
eyes.bio: The ILN gave most readers their only image of the stone in its old Mughal cut. Its own text conceded that the cut did not show off the stone's fire.

sources.title: V&A blog (reproduces ILN, 31 May 1851)

eyes.name: Household Words and The Household Narrative of Current Events (conducted by Charles Dickens), unsigned contributors
eyes.role: Weekly magazine and its monthly news supplement
eyes.authenticity: Contemporary issues digitised by Dickens Journals Online. The pieces were unsigned. The Household Words page is assigned to the 2 August 1851 issue by the site's date list, not by a printed date on the page.
eyes.bio: Dickens's magazines reached a wide middle-class readership. One reported the gift as news, with a fabulous valuation. The other made the Exhibition display into a comic sketch about security rather than beauty.

sources.title: Household Narrative of Current Events, 1850, p. 164 (DJO)
Household Words, vol. III (1851), p. 437 (DJO)

eyes.name: Sir David Brewster
eyes.role: Scottish physicist, authority on the optics of crystals; Principal of the United College, St Andrews

waypoints.label: London: examines the stone for Prince Albert, 1852

eyes.authenticity: 'Observations on the Koh-i-noor diamond', read to the British Association at Belfast in 1852 and printed in its report (1853); summarised in Scientific American in November 1852.
eyes.bio: Prince Albert asked Brewster to look inside the stone before anyone cut it. Under polarised light and the microscope he found flaws and tiny cavities, which made recutting risky. His report treats the gem as a specimen, not a trophy.

sources.title: Scientific American, 13 November 1852: British Association report

eyes.name: James Tennant
eyes.role: Mineralogist and dealer, Professor of Mineralogy at King's College London; mineralogist to the Queen
eyes.authenticity: His warning before the cutting is reported in The Times, 19 July 1852. His paper 'On the recutting of the Koh-i-noor' was given to the British Association at Liverpool in 1854 and printed in its report and the American Journal of Science.
eyes.bio: Tennant was among the experts consulted on whether the stone could be cut safely. With Professor Mitchell he warned of the risk of cutting from the side. He attended the work and afterwards gave the scientific account of the stone's loss of weight.

sources.title: GIA: Koh-i-Noor diamond reading list (Tennant 1854; Brewster 1853)
Understanding Jewellery: Amsterdam's magnificent diamond legacy, Part I

eyes.name: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto
eyes.vantage_label: a successor state asking for it back
eyes.authenticity: His 1976 letter to James Callaghan is reported in later press accounts; its full text was not seen for this chapter.
eyes.bio: Bhutto made the first formal request from a Pakistani head of government. Lahore, where the treaty was signed, is in Pakistan. His letter stands here for the state claims that began in 1947 and still go on.

sources.title: The News Minute: India and the legacy of the Kohinoor diamond

entries.place: The darbar in the Lahore citadel
entries.headline: A ten-year-old signs away a kingdom and its diamond
entries.digest: Six weeks after the Sikh defeat at Gujrat, the boy Maharaja sat in darbar while the British terms were read: the Punjab annexed, the state property confiscated, and the Koh-i-Noor named separately for surrender to the Queen. He put his signature to the document beside those of his surviving ministers. He was given a pension and removed from power. No word of his own from that day survives.
entries.source_note: Treaty of Lahore, 29 March 1849, Article III (text as quoted in Dalrymple and Anand, Kohinoor, preview PDF, and The Conversation); date in all sources.

entries.headline: Dalhousie owns the annexation as his own act
entries.digest: The day after the signing, Dalhousie wrote to his friend Sir George Couper. He had annexed the Punjab without waiting for authority from London, and said so plainly. He accepted the responsibility and called the step just, prudent and unavoidable. He expected argument at home and dared his critics to it.
entries.quote: What I have done I have done on my own responsibility.
entries.source_note: Dalhousie to Couper, 30 March 1849, Private Letters (1910), as quoted in The Conversation.

entries.headline: A surgeon takes the keys to Ranjit Singh's treasury
entries.digest: Login was put in charge of the citadel and the Toshakhana, where the jewels, arms, shawls and relics of the Sikh court were stored. With the old treasury officials he began a long inventory. The Koh-i-Noor was the one item set apart by treaty. His letters to his wife describe the scale of the hoard and the care taken over every seal.
entries.source_note: Lady Login, Sir John Login and Duleep Singh (1890), as summarised in Login's biography; month of appointment from secondary sources.

entries.headline: The Company's directors resent losing the stone to the Crown
entries.digest: Couper had warned him that the Court of Directors were annoyed that the treaty gave the Koh-i-Noor to the Queen and not to the Company. Dalhousie answered at length. In his view the stone, as a symbol of conquest, belonged to the sovereign, and a gift direct from the Maharaja honoured her more than one passed through the Company. He was sure he had served the Queen's dignity and would not back down.
entries.quote: The Court, you say, are ruffled
entries.source_note: Dalhousie to Couper, 16 August 1849, Private Letters (1910), quoted in The Conversation. Place: Dalhousie spent the 1849 hot season at Simla (approx).

entries.headline: Dalhousie signs for the Koh-i-Noor in person
entries.digest: On a cold December day Dalhousie came to Lahore and took the stone from Login. He signed a receipt stating that he had received the diamond that day. Lady Dalhousie sewed it into a belt for him, and he wore it on his journey south. The transfer turned a treaty clause into an object in one man's keeping.
entries.source_note: Dalrymple and Anand, Kohinoor (2017), preview PDF (receipt, December 1849, day not given); belt story widely repeated in secondary accounts.

entries.headline: Login hands over the stone he has guarded
entries.digest: Login's keeping of the diamond ended when he handed it to the Governor-General. In the family tradition his widow recorded, the old treasury staff had taught him how the stone was wrapped and handled, and he followed their method to the end. His relief at being rid of the responsibility comes through in the later account.
entries.source_note: Dalrymple and Anand preview (Dalhousie took delivery from Dr Login); Lady Login (1890) for the Login side; day not established.

entries.headline: The waistcoat pocket and the tin box: a later story
entries.digest: In a story told long afterwards, Lawrence was given the little box holding the stone, put it in his waistcoat pocket, changed clothes and forgot it. When an urgent request came weeks later he asked his old bearer, who produced the box from a tin trunk. The bearer reportedly saw nothing in it but a bit of glass. The anecdote is not supported by any contemporary document and does not fit the record of Dalhousie taking the stone himself in December.
entries.source_note: Later anecdote, labelled as such: retold in Anglo-Indian biography and popular histories; The Week (2022), drawing on Dalrymple and Anand, notes no contemporary evidence.

entries.headline: Dalhousie orders an inquiry into the diamond's past
entries.digest: Within days of taking the stone, Dalhousie wrote a minute ordering officials to collect what could be learned of its history, so that a provenance could go to the Queen with it. The work went to Theophilus Metcalfe at Delhi, who gathered court traditions and bazaar stories. Most later popular histories of the stone, including the tales of its curse, draw on what he collected.
entries.source_note: National Archives of India, Foreign Dept 1849, 'Orders for the collection of information re: the history of the Kohinoor', minute by Dalhousie dated 22 December 1849; Metcalfe commission per Dalrymple and Anand preview.

entries.headline: Carried by hand to Bombay, locked in the treasury
entries.digest: Dalhousie wrote to the Queen that he had brought the diamond from Lahore himself and that day placed it in the Bombay treasury. It would stay there for two months until a warship could take it. He kept the plan secret and told almost no one when the stone would sail.
entries.source_note: Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 31734 (Koh-i-nûr armlet), citing Dalhousie's letter to Queen Victoria of 1 February 1850.

entries.headline: The stone goes aboard a small steam sloop
entries.digest: The stone was carried aboard HMS Medea under Commander William Lockyer. Only Lockyer and the two escorts, Ramsay and Mackeson, knew what was in the box, which needed several keys to open. Ramsay reported to Dalhousie from the harbour that the gem was safely on board.
entries.source_note: Sailing date in Dalrymple and Anand (via Victorian Web review) and secondary accounts; Ramsay's letter from Bombay Harbour, NAI Foreign Dept 72–92 of 1850 No. 89 (catalogued 14 June 1850, a date that does not fit the sailing).

entries.headline: Cholera breaks out on board
entries.digest: About ten days out of Bombay, cholera appeared among the crew. Men fell sick in the cramped ship, and secondary accounts report that two of the crew died. The secret cargo made no difference to a disease that the sailors had no means to stop.
entries.source_note: Dalrymple and Anand (via Victorian Web review: 'about ten days' after sailing); death toll from secondary popular accounts, not verified in a primary source.

entries.headline: Mauritius refuses the plague ship
entries.digest: Short of coal, the Medea put in at Mauritius. The island's authorities, fearing the cholera, refused to deal with her and ordered her away. Lockyer refused to leave, and in the popular account the local authorities threatened to fire on the ship. Coal was finally supplied and she sailed on.
entries.source_note: Secondary accounts (thebizdom.in; famouskohinoordiamond blog) based on Dalrymple and Anand; the escort letters in NAI series 72–92 of 1850 not read in full.

entries.headline: A twelve-hour gale on the last leg
entries.digest: On the way north the Medea ran into a storm that lasted about twelve hours and battered the small ship. The escorts' letters later disagreed on details of the trip. Neither recorded any danger to the box itself.
entries.source_note: Secondary accounts; NAI catalogue notes that Mackeson's and Ramsay's letters give differing accounts of the trip.

entries.headline: Landfall in England after twelve weeks
entries.digest: The Medea reached Plymouth. The escorts went on with the box to Portsmouth and then by train to London. The Company's officials met them there and took charge of the keys.
entries.source_note: Dalrymple and Anand (via Victorian Web review) and Indian Culture/NVLI story (arrival in England 29–30 June).

entries.place: East India House, Leadenhall Street, London
entries.headline: The Company signs a receipt for the stone
entries.digest: Mackeson and Ramsay delivered the box to the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Court of Directors, John Shepherd and J. W. Hogg, who signed a formal receipt. The Company that had wanted the stone for itself now held it for one day as the Queen's courier.
entries.source_note: NAI Foreign Dept receipt Nos. 182–186 (receipt signed on delivery; catalogued 23 August 1850); delivery date from Indian Culture/NVLI story.

entries.headline: The Queen receives the stone, and is not dazzled
entries.digest: The Company's chairman and deputy chairman presented the diamond to the Queen at the palace, in the Company's 250th year. In her journal she admired its size but noted that it was badly cut, and that its setting was closed behind, which dulled it. The ceremony came days after a man had struck her with a cane in public, and her entry places the gem among other events.
entries.source_note: Presentation date: RCT RCIN 31734 and Household Narrative (July 1850). Journal wording known from Dalrymple and Anand, p. 216, via Victorian Web review; exact date of the journal entry not seen (approx).

entries.headline: Dickens's news digest prices the gift at two millions
entries.digest: The monthly Household Narrative reported that the chairman and deputy chairman had presented the Koh-i-Noor to the Queen at the levee on the 3rd. It gave a potted history from the Golconda mines through the Mughals to the Sikh war. It valued the stone at a sum no one could check, which showed how much the British public had heard about it before anyone had seen it.
entries.quote: presented to the queen at the levee on the 3rd
entries.source_note: Household Narrative of Current Events, 1850, p. 164 (Dickens Journals Online); issue month inferred from the site's date list.

entries.headline: The Exhibition opens with the diamond in its cage
entries.digest: The Queen opened the Great Exhibition and wrote of it as one of the proudest days of her life, the triumph of her husband's project. The Koh-i-Noor was on show in the centre of the nave in a gilded iron cage, on a red cushion, over a safe into which it could drop if anyone touched the glass. It was one of the Exhibition's most advertised exhibits.
entries.source_note: Journal sentiment as quoted in Dalrymple and Anand, p. 219 (via Victorian Web review); display arrangements from V&A blog.

entries.headline: The picture press shows the stone in its Mughal cut
entries.digest: The Illustrated London News printed an engraving of the Koh-i-Noor between the two lesser diamonds that had come with it in Ranjit Singh's armlet. The picture showed the stone as it was presented to the Queen. Readers saw a lumpy, shallow shape rather than the sparkling brilliant they expected. In its coverage the paper admitted that the stone was not cut in the best form to show its lustre.
entries.source_note: ILN 31 May 1851 engraving, reproduced on V&A blog and cited by the wheatoneng235 blog; 'not cut in the best form' quoted from ILN in Dalrymple and Anand, p. 223 (issue date of that remark not seen).

entries.headline: Crowds doubt the famous diamond is real
entries.digest: The Times reported that many visitors, after queueing to see the stone, could not believe that the dull object under the glass was the famous diamond. The disappointment had become a running story of the Exhibition. The organisers came under pressure to do something about the display.
entries.quote: many people find a difficulty in bringing themselves to believe
entries.source_note: The Times, 13 June 1851, quoted on V&A blog.

entries.headline: The royal couple go straight to the diamond
entries.digest: After the complaints, the stone was moved into a small dark enclosure lit by gas jets and backed by mirrors. The Queen and Prince Albert came to the Exhibition and went first to see the new arrangement. They took charge of the problem themselves.
entries.source_note: V&A blog (visit of 14 June 1851).

entries.headline: Gaslight and mirrors fail to rescue it
entries.digest: Two days after the royal visit, The Times judged the new lighting a failure. Under gas lamps and a dozen small mirrors the stone still looked dull. The paper's verdict made recutting the obvious next step.
entries.source_note: The Times, 16 June 1851, quoted on V&A blog.

entries.headline: A comic visitor dreams of stealing it
entries.digest: A sketch in Household Words followed a visitor who found the diamond itself no match for his imagination. What impressed him was the security: a bell-glass, an iron cage, clockwork and a policeman. He kept coming back and plotting a theft, and decided only a master thief could succeed. The joke was that the stone's guards had become the real show.
entries.quote: thief of the very highest genius
entries.source_note: Household Words, vol. III (1851), p. 437 (Dickens Journals Online); issue date inferred from the site's date list.

entries.headline: From India, Dalhousie blames the cutting
entries.digest: Hearing of the disappointment in London, Dalhousie wrote that the problem was the stone's old-fashioned cut. It was a rose cut, not a brilliant, and he said it was never going to sparkle in the way the crowds expected. In his view the stone was not at fault; the fault lay with the people who had shaped it centuries earlier.
entries.source_note: Dalhousie letter of 1851 quoted on famouskohinoordiamond blog; not checked against the 1910 edition; exact date unknown.

entries.headline: The Exhibition's great disappointment, in retrospect
entries.digest: As the Exhibition closed, The Times looked back and named the Koh-i-Noor as the biggest letdown of the whole show, out of all proportion to its size. The paper's view was that the stone's fame had raised expectations it could never meet.
entries.source_note: The Times, 13 October 1851, paraphrased on V&A blog.

entries.headline: The organiser slips the diamond into his pocket
entries.digest: Two days after the Exhibition closed, Cole recorded the removal of the stone from its display. He examined it closely and, for a moment, held it in his own pocket, and he noted this with obvious delight in a crowded day's entry. He was writing about an object, not a symbol.
entries.source_note: Henry Cole diary, 17 October 1851 (National Art Library, V&A), transcribed on V&A blog.

entries.headline: Polarised light reveals hidden flaws
entries.digest: At Prince Albert's request Brewster examined the stone under polarised light and the microscope before any cutting began. He saw bands of strain and tiny internal cavities ringed by polarisation. He thought they had been formed by gas or fluid under pressure. His findings meant that a careless cut could split the gem.
entries.source_note: Brewster, 'Observations on the Koh-i-noor', British Association Report (1853); GIA reading list; date of examination given only as before the recutting.

entries.headline: The experts' warning before the wheel turns
entries.digest: Tennant and Professor Mitchell had warned that cutting the stone from the side could endanger it. The Amsterdam firm of Coster judged the risk manageable. Coster's men, led by Levie Benjamin Voorzanger with J. A. Fedder, worked at a wheel driven by a small steam engine. Tennant attended the work as the Queen's mineralogist.
entries.source_note: The Times, 19 July 1852, reprinted in New Zealand Spectator, 8 December 1852 (Papers Past); workmen's names from Understanding Jewellery.

entries.headline: The Iron Duke cuts the first facet
entries.digest: On the Friday afternoon the Duke of Wellington, now 83, came to Garrard's. The stone was set in lead with one corner left exposed, and he held it to the turning wheel until that corner was ground away and the first new facet was cut. Sebastian Garrard missed the moment: he had fallen through an opening in the floor while the engine was being installed and broken his leg. The paper expected the work to take months and not to reduce the weight much.
entries.quote: the first facet of the new cutting was effected
entries.source_note: The Times, Monday 19 July 1852 ('Friday afternoon' = 16 July), reprinted in New Zealand Spectator, 8 December 1852; Spectator (London), 24 July 1852, p. 14.

entries.headline: A scientist reports the diamond's inner cavities
entries.digest: Brewster read his observations to the British Association in Belfast while the recut stone was already being finished. He described the cavities and a yellowish substance in a pit left by the old gold setting. He compared the stone with other diamonds that held trapped matter, using the famous gem as evidence about how diamonds form.
entries.source_note: Scientific American, 13 November 1852, reporting the British Association; GIA reading list (Belfast, September 1852).

entries.headline: A smaller, brighter stone comes back to the Queen
entries.digest: After thirty-eight days of cutting, the work begun in July was completed and the stone returned as an oval brilliant. It had lost a large share of its weight, and Prince Albert was reportedly troubled by how much smaller it was. Garrard's mounted it for the Queen, who wore it as a brooch and had it painted into her portrait by Winterhalter.
entries.source_note: RCT RCIN 31734 (recutting July–September 1852; settings by Garrard); duration from Encyclopaedia Iranica and Understanding Jewellery; no journal entry for the return seen.

entries.headline: The young Maharaja sits for Winterhalter
entries.digest: Duleep Singh, now fifteen and newly arrived in England, sat to Winterhalter at the palace for a full-length portrait. The Queen recorded that the painter was in raptures over the boy's looks and bearing, and that Duleep sat patiently for more than two hours. She had already privately asked Lady Login whether he ever mentioned the diamond.
entries.source_note: Queen Victoria's journal, 10 July 1854, quoted by Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 403843; the question to Lady Login from Lady Login (1890) via The Tribune.

entries.headline: Will he throw it out of the window?
entries.digest: Lady Login recalled that, during one of the sittings, the Queen came in with the recut diamond and a guard of Yeomen and put it into Duleep Singh's hand. He turned it over at the window for long minutes. She feared he would do something rash, even throw it out. Instead he crossed the room, bowed and handed it back, saying it gave him great pleasure to offer it to his sovereign himself.
entries.source_note: Lady Login, Sir John Login and Duleep Singh (1890), as summarised in The Tribune and RCT RCIN 403843; written 36 years later; exact day not given.

entries.headline: Holding his father's diamond, smaller now
entries.digest: In Lady Login's telling, the boy noticed at once that the stone was smaller and brighter than the one he had known in Lahore. It was the first time he had held it since the surrender. He handed it back with courtly words. Whatever he felt was not written down by him at the time, and his later letters suggest it was not simple gratitude.
entries.source_note: Lady Login (1890) via The Tribune and Victorian Web review of Dalrymple and Anand, p. 247; his own words in 1854 known only through her.

entries.headline: The recut stone lent for a charity evening
entries.digest: Cole noted a conversazione at his museum to raise money for the Female School of Art, which had lost its government grant. The Queen lent the Koh-i-Noor, shown alongside the Hope diamond, and he counted more than twelve hundred guests. By then the stone was a crowd-pleaser to be lent out, no longer a war prize.
entries.source_note: Henry Cole diary, 21 June 1860, transcribed on V&A blog.

entries.headline: Measuring what the wheel took away
entries.digest: Tennant gave the British Association a technical account of the recutting. The stone had been reduced from about 186 carats to a little over 100. He defended the result as the price of turning a lumpy relic into a stone that could sparkle. He also described the removal of a flaw that had threatened it.
entries.source_note: Tennant, 'On the recutting of the Koh-i-noor', British Association Report (Liverpool, 1854); GIA reading list summary. Exact figures in Tennant's paper not seen.

entries.headline: The exile tells The Times he was robbed
entries.digest: Deep in debt and at odds with the India Office over his pension and estates, Duleep Singh wrote to The Times to state his case in public. He argued that the annexation of 1849 had been an injustice to a child under British protection. The letter marks his public break with the gratitude Lady Login would later describe.
entries.quote: I have been most unjustly deprived of my kingdom
entries.source_note: Duleep Singh to The Times, August 1882, quoted in Historic Royal Palaces source booklet (2014); day not given.

entries.headline: Stopped at Aden, he returns to the Sikh faith
entries.digest: Setting out for India against the government's wishes, Duleep Singh was detained at Aden by British officials. There he took Sikh initiation again, renouncing the Christianity of his boyhood. In letters of this period he denounced the Queen's title to the Punjab and accused the British of taking his kingdom by fraud. He was not allowed to go on to India and spent his last years in Paris.
entries.source_note: Historic Royal Palaces, Duleep Singh pages and source booklet (letter to the Prince of Wales, undated); month of the Aden ceremony not verified here.

entries.headline: Pakistan asks Britain for the diamond
entries.digest: Bhutto wrote to the British prime minister, James Callaghan, asking for the Koh-i-Noor to be returned to Pakistan. He cited the stone's great sentimental value and its history in Lahore. The British government declined, and the reply referred to the 1849 treaty and the competing claims of other states.
entries.source_note: The News Minute (2015), citing press reports of the 1976 letter; text of the letter and of the reply not seen.

convergences.label: The Treaty of Lahore and the morning after
convergences.note: The boy signs in silence at Lahore; a day later Dalhousie writes from the frontier that the act is his own and he will answer for it. Only the winner's voice survives from that week.

convergences.label: The handover in Lahore
convergences.note: Dalhousie's receipt and Login's family memory agree that the Governor-General took the stone in person. The Lawrence waistcoat story, told long afterwards, sets a comic tale of forgetfulness against that documented sequence.

convergences.label: Presentation to the Queen
convergences.note: The escort signs the stone over to the Company on the 2nd. On the 3rd the Queen privately records its bad cut, while the popular press values it in millions.

convergences.label: The disappointment week at the Crystal Palace
convergences.note: The picture press shows the old cut, The Times reports public disbelief, and the royal couple come to inspect a gas-lit tent. Two days later the paper says it has not worked.

convergences.label: The Exhibition closes
convergences.note: The Times calls the stone the show's great letdown; four days later Cole is happily turning it over in his hand. The newspaper judged the stone by its fame, and Cole by the object itself.

convergences.label: The first cut at Garrard's
convergences.note: The press tells the story of the old Duke at the wheel; the scientists record the flaws and risks that made the work dangerous; Brewster's cavities are what Coster's men had to cut around.

convergences.label: The diamond back in Duleep Singh's hand
convergences.note: The Queen's journal records a handsome boy and a patient sitter; Lady Login, decades later, remembers fearing he would throw the stone away; Duleep's own feelings are not on the record until his angry letters of the 1880s.

ties.note: Login served under Dalhousie at Lahore and handed him the stone; Dalhousie then made him guardian of the Maharaja.
Captain James Ramsay was Dalhousie's kinsman and confidential agent, chosen to escort the stone because he could be trusted.
Lawrence sat on the Board of Administration Dalhousie created to govern the annexed Punjab.
The Governor-General who annexed the kingdom and the boy who lost it; Dalhousie's letters speak of him with condescension.
Dalhousie wrote to the Queen about the stone's journey; she received the gift he had insisted should be hers.
Husband and wife; her 1890 book preserves his Lahore letters.
She helped raise him at Fatehgarh and accompanied him to England in 1854.
The Queen made him a favourite at court in 1854 and handed him the recut stone; thirty years later he called her rule over the Punjab a fraud.
Cole worked with Prince Albert on the Exhibition; the Queen later lent the diamond to his museum.
Both were consulted by Prince Albert; Brewster's map of the flaws shaped the caution Tennant urged before cutting.
The Times reported Tennant's warning about cutting the stone from the side.
Pakistan's claim rests on Lahore, the capital where Duleep Singh signed the treaty.

threads_out.note: The Cullinan, like the recut Koh-i-Noor, was cut by an Amsterdam firm (Asscher, 1908) and became a British crown jewel. Amsterdam's cutters were called in for both stones, half a century apart.

The Koh-i-Noor's fame made the Indian diamond the model of a great stone. Within two decades the South African fields made large diamonds plentiful and moved the trade's centre from India and Brazil to the Cape.
Dalhousie's annexations, the Punjab among them, were widely blamed for the rising of 1857. John Lawrence governed the Punjab through it and sent Punjab troops to retake Delhi.
The cholera aboard HMS Medea in 1850, and Mauritius's refusal to receive the ship, belong to the second cholera pandemic and the quarantine fears traced in that chapter.
The stone's Mughal years link it to the jewel-hung court that Sir Thomas Roe described at Jahangir's darbar. Mughal treasure remained the European idea of Indian wealth into 1851.
